paper.title: Detecting an Odd Restless Markov Arm with a Trembling Hand

settings.name_in_paper: Odd arm identification with restless Markov arms and a trembling hand
unmapped: Odd arm identification: one arm has transition matrix P1, all others P2 != P1; goal is to find the odd arm with error probability <= epsilon (fixed confidence)
Each arm is an ergodic Markov chain on a common finite state space, arms evolve whether or not pulled (restless)
P1 and P2 are known to the learner
Trembling hand: intended arm pulled w.p. 1-eta, otherwise uniformly random arm, eta in (0,1]; actual arm is observed
settings.definition_quote: We consider a multi-armed bandit with $K\geq 3$ arms ... The Markovian evolution of states on one of the arms (known as the \emph{odd} arm) is governed by a transition probability matrix $P_1$, and the evolution of states on each of the non-odd arms is governed by $P_2$ ... the intended arm $B_{t}$ gets pulled with probability $1-\eta$ and a uniformly random arm gets pulled with probability $\eta$ ... The unobserved arms continue to undergo state evolution, making the arms \emph{restless}.

symbols.R_star: R^*(P_1,P_2): sup over stationary randomised policies of min over alternative odd arms h' of the sum over (delays, last states, arm) of the ergodic state-action occupancy measure times KL divergences of d-step transition laws

conditions: policies in Pi(epsilon): error probability <= epsilon for every odd arm location
P1 != P2 known, ergodic, same support

source.label: prop:lower_bound
source.quote: Let $\eta\in(0,1]$ and $h\in\mathcal{A}$ be fixed. Assume that $\mathcal{H}_h$ is the true hypothesis. ... Then, \liminf_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\epsilon)}\frac{E_h[\tau(\pi)]}{\log(1/\epsilon)}\geq \frac{1}{R^*(P_1,P_2)}

results.notes: Paper's epsilon (error probability) mapped to canonical delta.

symbols.delta_alg: the paper's policy parameter delta > 0 (approximation slack to the supremum)
symbols.L: threshold parameter of the policy; L = 1/epsilon gives error probability <= epsilon

source.label: prop:upper_bound
source.quote: Fix $h\in\mathcal{A}$ and $\delta>0$, and let $\mathcal{H}_h$ be the true hypothesis. The policy $\pi^\star(L, \delta)$ satisfies \limsup_{L\to\infty}\frac{E_h[\tau(\pi^\star(L, \delta))]}{\log L}\leq \frac{1+\delta}{R^*(P_1,P_2)}.

results.notes: With L = 1/epsilon (Lemma 3) the policy is epsilon-correct, so log L = log(1/delta) in canonical notation.

source.label: lem:pi_star(L)_in_Pi(epsilon)
source.quote: Fix error probability $\epsilon>0$. If $L=1/\epsilon$, then for every $\delta>0$, $\pi^\star(L,\delta)\in\Pi(\epsilon)$.

results.notes: Error probability at stoppage <= epsilon (canonical delta); proof shows <= 1/L. Probability field set loosely.

conditions: arms are time-homogeneous ergodic Markov chains on a finite state space

source.label: prop:main_result
source.quote: Consider a multi-armed bandit with $K\geq 3$ arms in which each arm is a time homogeneous and ergodic Markov process ... the expected time required by the decision maker to identify the odd arm satisfies the asymptotic relation \lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\epsilon)}\frac{E_h[\tau(\pi)]}{\log(1/\epsilon)}=\lim_{\delta \downarrow 0}\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{E_h[\tau(\pi^\star(L,\delta))]}{\log L}= \frac{1}{R^*(P_1,P_2)}.

results.notes: Theorem is an exact limit equality (matching lower bound Prop 1); recorded as the upper (achievability) side, which is asymptotically optimal.
